newsitem.title: USA: Lawmakers blast Social Security Web site privacy.
newsitem.headline: Lawmakers blast Social Security Web site privacy.

text.p: Lawmakers Wednesday warned the government to stop posting sensitive Social Security data on the Internet, charging that the confidential financial records of millions of Americans had been put at risk.

Pennsylvania Democratic Rep. Paul Kanjorski announced he would introduce a bill to bar the Social Security Administration from posting earnings and benefit estimate statements on a special Internet Web site.
Kentucky Republican Rep. Jim Bunning, chair of the House Ways and Means subcommittee that oversees the SSA, wrote to the agency asking for a thorough review of the service.
"While I appreciate SSA's desire to provide fast and expedient service, such action should not compromise the privacy of Americans," Bunning told the agency.
"Americans trust that their records will be kept safe and secure. I fear such trust will quickly erode, unless the public can be assured their records are protected," he said.
Bunning asked for a response by April 22 and said he was prepared to hold hearings to address the issue.
The SSA last month began offering a new service on the Internet, designed to make it easier for people to get access to their financial records and plan for retirement.
Using a name, Social Security number, mother's maiden name, birthdate and place of birth, an individual can look up decades of past earnings records and projected Social Security benefits.
Some privacy experts have said it may be too easy for scam artists or nosy friends and relatives to gain access to the confidential information.
The SSA says it is confident the data is secure, but is reviewing the Web site. In the past, people wanting such information had to go to a local Social Security office or write to the agency.
"We are monitoring and evaluating the use of the Web site and the security measures that are protecting it," said Rich Hensley, an SSA spokesperson.

Hensley said the Web site had been getting about 3,000 queries a day since the data was made available about a month ago. It got 85,000 Tuesday, probably due in part to a spate of news reports about the data and possible privacy concerns.
In fact, some people who have tried to look at their records have been unable to gain access because so many people are trying to view the site.
